newsitem.title: UK: British business chiefs warn on Euroscepticism.
newsitem.headline: British business chiefs warn on Euroscepticism.

text.p: A group of top British industrialists have said they are dismayed by hostility towards the European Union (EU) in the run-up to an election expected to be held on May 1.

In a letter published on Tuesday in the Financial Times, the business leaders said they had "watched with dismay the spread of extreme Euroscepticism", arguing that Britain would suffer economically if it became more distant from the EU.

Sir Colin Marshall, president of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) and chairman of British Airways Plc, and 22 others said they were concerned that the debate on EU policy was being turned into a debate about membership of the bloc.

A similar FT letter last year called for Britain not to rule out permanently joining a single European currency. It comes amid growing dissent within Britain's ruling Conservative party over policy towards Europe.

Ten of the signatories to last year's letter added their names to the latest letter to the Financial Times, which Sir Colin told the paper had arisen from "conversations" between the individuals with some co-ordination by the CBI.

Pointing out that nearly 60 percent of Britain's visible trade is with EU members and that more than 2,000 continental European firms had invested here, the letter said such advances will be at risk if Euroscepticism continues to gain pace.
"These benefits would be put at risk if this country chose the path of isolation," the letter said. "Britain would be a poorer place, with lower investment and higher unemployment."
It said Britain needs to demonstrate that its commitment to Europe is not in doubt.
If it fails to do so, Britain's position in the EU's forthcoming inter-governmental conference on the move towards a single European currency will be "seriously compromised," the letter said.

Niall Fitzgerald, chairman of the Anglo-Dutch consumer products group Unilever Plc and one of the FT letter signatories, last month warned that the company might review its investment in Britain if the government failed to join a single currency.
Fitzgerald's comments echoed an earlier warning by Japanese auto group Toyota that it might reconsider investment in Britain if it was outside monetary union.

Other signatories of the latest FT letter included British Telecommunications Plc chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield, B.A.T Industries Plc chief executive Martin Broughton, and British Petroleum Co Plc chairman Sir David Simon.
